summary: This paper investigates whether the internal representations of large reasoning models encode information about the relative long-horizon value of alternative next-token candidates. The authors construct the Reasoning Candidate-Token Value (RCTV) dataset and show that relative candidate value is linearly decodable from hidden states, MLP outputs, and attention outputs. Furthermore, they demonstrate that using these decoded signals to guide token selection during generation improves the chances of eventual success in online interventions.

Linear Decodability of Candidate Value

We evaluate candidate-value readout from representations at the candidate-token position. We repeat
five-fold cross-validation with ten problem-level
fold seeds and examine hidden state, MLP output,
and self-attention output representations across layers and numbers of selected dimensions.
Candidate-value signal is unevenly distributed across layers and dimensions, with different patterns across representation families.
Figure 2 shows the mean pairwise AUC over ten
problem-level fold seeds for each layer and number
of selected dimensions. Hidden states show higher
pairwise AUC mainly in middle-to-late layers, with
a weaker signal in early layers at high dimensionality. MLP outputs exhibit peaks with very few
selected dimensions, particularly near layers 9 and
17. Attention outputs show more scattered regions
of higher pairwise AUC. Appendix G further shows
heatmaps of standard deviation and above-chance
frequency across fold seeds.
Candidate-value readout can outperform
probability-, rank- and embedding-based baselines. Table 2 reports the strongest observed configuration in each representation family according
to mean pairwise AUC. All three families achieve
higher pairwise and tier AUC and lower Regret@1
than the probability, rank, and embedding baselines.

readout achieves the highest tier AUC. The MLP
